question: What is a polar high altitude en route chart mainly used for?

options.text: VFR navigation over Greenland and northern Canada below the lowest airways
Planning flights between Europe and Africa over the Mediterranean region
Approach and landing at aerodromes north of the Arctic Circle in poor visibility and darkness
Planning routes and high-altitude polar navigation between Europe and North America

explanation: The chart is used mainly for route planning and high-altitude polar navigation between Europe and North America.

question: Between which levels are flights from Europe to the Canadian Arctic strongly recommended to plan on the polar track structure, at the published times?

options.text: FL245 to FL460 inclusive
FL290 to FL410 inclusive
FL195 to FL660 inclusive
FL280 to FL390 inclusive

explanation: Operations between Europe and the Canadian Arctic between FL280 and FL390 inclusive are strongly recommended to flight plan on the polar track structure at the published times.

question: How many fixed tracks does the polar track structure have in the Reykjavik control area?
explanation: There are 10 fixed tracks in the Reykjavik CTA and 5 through the Bodø oceanic area, which continue the relevant Reykjavik tracks.

question: On what projection is a polar high altitude chart drawn?

options.text: Lambert conformal conic
Transverse Mercator
Direct Mercator
Polar stereographic

explanation: The polar high altitude chart is a polar stereographic projection.

question: Which property does a polar stereographic chart have in polar regions?

options.text: Great circles are nearly straight lines and scale is nearly constant
Rhumb lines are straight lines and meridians are parallel lines
Scale is correct only along the standard parallel at 60°N and nowhere else on the chart
Bearings are correct only along the central meridian of the chart

explanation: Bearings are correct (it is conformal); near the pole great circles are straight lines and the scale is constant and correct.

question: Why is magnetic direction impractical in high latitudes?

options.text: Compasses cannot be fitted to aircraft that fly above FL280
The isogonals are not printed on charts north of 70°N
The magnetic pole always lies at the geographic pole, so all variation is zero
Variation changes rapidly and the compass directive force falls towards zero

explanation: Near the magnetic pole, variation changes rapidly over short distances and the horizontal directive force that aligns the compass needle reduces towards zero.

question: To what are VORs in very high latitudes, such as near the magnetic pole, often aligned?

options.text: Magnetic north
Compass north
True north
Grid north

explanation: In high latitudes VORs cannot sensibly be referenced to local magnetic north, so some are aligned with true north.

question: Why are true tracks also unsuitable for navigation in high latitudes?

options.text: The meridians converge rapidly, so true track changes quickly along a straight line
Inertial systems cannot measure true direction above 70° of latitude
True tracks always differ by exactly 180° between the outbound and the return legs of a route
True north cannot be shown on any chart drawn on a polar stereographic projection

explanation: Rapid convergence of the meridians makes the true direction of a straight track change rapidly over short distances.

question: On a polar chart, why is the return true track of a leg not the reciprocal of the outbound true track?

options.text: The variation changes between the two ends of the leg
The meridians converge, so the track crosses them at different angles at each end
The wind is different on the return leg
The leg is drawn as a rhumb line on a polar chart, not as a great circle

explanation: Because meridians converge, a straight track has a different true direction at each end, so the return true track is not the outbound one plus 180°. The grid tracks are (almost) reciprocal.

question: Which datum gives a constant track direction along a straight line on a polar chart?

options.text: Compass north
Magnetic north
True north
Grid north

explanation: Grid north is a fixed direction across the chart, so a straight track keeps a constant grid direction.

question: On a typical polar stereographic chart, which meridian is used as the grid north datum?

options.text: The Greenwich meridian
The 180° meridian
The meridian through the departure point
The 90°W meridian

explanation: The Greenwich meridian is the grid datum, highlighted with a thick line, with grid lines parallel to it at 300 NM intervals.

question: What is convergence, in grid navigation?

options.text: The angle between true north and magnetic north
The angle between true north and grid north at a point
The change of longitude along a track between two points
The angle between grid north and compass north

explanation: Convergence is the angular difference between true and grid direction at a point on a grid chart.

question: Which rule converts true direction to grid direction?

options.text: Convergence west, grid best; convergence east, grid least
Convergence east, true best; convergence west, true least
Convergence west, true best; convergence east, true least
Always add the convergence, whether it is east or west

explanation: With westerly convergence true is greater than grid (true best, grid least); with easterly convergence true is less (true least, grid best).

question: On a north polar stereographic chart with the Greenwich grid datum, what is the convergence at a point?

options.text: Half the longitude of the point
The longitude with its sign changed
The longitude with the same sign as the longitude
The latitude of the point

explanation: On such a chart the convergence equals the longitude with the sign changed: at 40°E the convergence is 40°W.

question: Which simple formula gives grid direction on a north polar chart with a Greenwich datum?

options.text: Grid = true + longitude west, or − longitude east
Grid = true − longitude west, or + longitude east
Grid = magnetic + longitude west, or − longitude east
Grid = true + variation west, or − variation east

explanation: Grid bearing equals true bearing plus west longitude or minus east longitude.

question: At 85°N 40°E the true track is 310°. What is the grid track?
explanation: Grid = true − longitude east = 310 − 40 = 270°(G).

question: At 85°N 40°W the true track is 230°. What is the grid track?
explanation: Grid = true + longitude west = 230 + 40 = 270°(G).

question: At 78°N 60°W the true track is 100°. What is the grid track?
explanation: Grid = true + longitude west = 100 + 60 = 160°(G).

question: At 80°N 30°E the grid track is 090°. What is the true track?
explanation: Grid = true − longitude east, so true = grid + 30 = 120°(T).

question: Where the track crosses the Greenwich meridian on a polar chart with a Greenwich datum, how do true and grid tracks compare?

options.text: They differ by the variation at that point
They differ by 90°, as the meridians are perpendicular
They are the same, as convergence is zero there
They differ by 180°, as the grid datum is reversed

explanation: Convergence equals the longitude with sign changed, so on the Greenwich meridian it is zero and true equals grid.

question: At longitude 30°W the true bearing is 337°. What is the grid bearing?
explanation: Grid = true + longitude west = 337 + 30 = 367 = 007°(G).

question: Which of these is a reason for using grid navigation in high latitudes?

options.text: Inertial systems cannot give true heading there
Grid direction is the same as magnetic direction
Charts in polar regions have no meridians printed on them at all
Magnetic compasses lose their directional accuracy

explanation: Grid is used because of rapid convergence of the meridians, rapid change of variation and the degraded directional ability of magnetic compasses.

question: On what projection are the North Atlantic plotting charts drawn?

options.text: Direct Mercator
Lambert conformal conic
Polar stereographic
Gnomonic with a tangent point at the pole

explanation: The plotting charts are Lambert conformal conic projections, on which scale is considered constant and straight lines are taken as great circles.

question: On the Lambert plotting charts, what is a straight line taken to be for practical purposes?

options.text: A great circle
A line of constant heading
A parallel of latitude
A rhumb line

explanation: For practical purposes a straight line on the Lambert plotting chart is a great circle, and bearings are correct.

question: What are the North Atlantic blow-up plotting charts designed for?

options.text: VFR navigation over the coastal areas on each side of the ocean below the airways
Approach and landing at the main transatlantic diversion aerodromes
Planning the polar track structure through the Arctic control areas
Extended twin operations, equal time point plotting and position plotting

explanation: They are designed for ETOPS, equal time point (critical point) calculation and plotting, and route and position plotting.

question: Which still-air range circles are shown round the North Atlantic diversion aerodromes on the blow-up chart?

options.text: 400 NM/60 min and 800 NM/120 min
820 NM/120 min and 1220 NM/180 min
1000 NM/150 min and 1500 NM/240 min
600 NM/90 min and 900 NM/138 min

explanation: The circles are 820 NM/120 minutes (at 410 kt) and 1220 NM/180 minutes (at about 406 kt), centred on diversion aerodromes open 24 hours.

question: A 120-minute still-air range circle has a radius of 820 NM. What TAS does it assume?

options.text: 420 kt
410 kt
400 kt
406 kt

explanation: 820 NM in 2 hours is 410 kt.

question: On an ETP plotting chart, what does every point on the midpoint line between two aerodromes represent?

options.text: The point where the 120-minute circles touch
A still-air equal time point, as it is equidistant from both
An equal time point in the forecast wind for the route at the planned level
The point of safe return from either aerodrome

explanation: Any point on the midpoint line is equidistant from the two aerodromes, so it is the still-air ETP/CP.

question: On an ETP plotting chart, what is the graticule at right angles to the midpoint line used for?

options.text: Plotting the aircraft's position from two DME ranges
Measuring the distance from the midpoint to each of the two aerodromes on the route
Adjusting the still-air ETP for the wind, towards ON or HOME
Finding the magnetic variation along the midpoint line

explanation: The graticule is used to move the still-air ETP for the wind, in the continuing (ON) or returning (HOME) direction.

question: How can distance be measured on an Atlantic orientation chart?

options.text: Only from the tables of distances printed in the chart's front information panel
Only by counting the latitude graticule squares crossed by the track
Only by computing the great circle distance from the co-ordinates
From the printed segment distances, the margin NM scale, or the adjacent meridian

explanation: Distances can be taken from the values printed parallel to the tracks, the nautical mile scale in the margins or the adjacent meridian scale.

question: Which of these is printed on the information panels of the Atlantic orientation charts?

options.text: Communication failure procedures and crossing clearance procedures
The take-off performance of the main aircraft types
Approach minima for every aerodrome shown on the chart, by aircraft category
The fuel prices at the oceanic diversion aerodromes

explanation: The panels include navaid lists, VOLMET, MNPS and the organised track system, communications and failure procedures, crossing clearance procedures, position reporting, contingency procedures and transponder use.

question: What equipment does RVSM airspace require?

options.text: One altimeter, a transponder with Mode A only and a radio altimeter for terrain
Two independent altitude measuring systems, an automatic altitude control and an altitude alerter
A single altimeter calibrated every flight against the destination QNH
Two inertial navigation systems coupled to the autopilot and a separate GNSS receiver for back-up

explanation: RVSM needs two fully serviceable independent altitude measurement systems, one automatic altitude-control system and one altitude-alerting device, plus Mode C SSR in radar-controlled transition airspace.

question: Within what tolerance must two primary altimeters agree in RVSM airspace?

options.text: ±75 ft

explanation: When altimeters are checked, pre-flight or in flight, at least two primary altimeters must agree within ±200 ft.

question: What navigation equipment does North Atlantic MNPS airspace require?

options.text: One GNSS receiver coupled to the autopilot
One long range navigation system and a VOR receiver for cross-checks
Two fully serviceable long range navigation systems
Two VOR receivers and a DME

explanation: Aircraft need two fully serviceable long range navigation systems (INS, GNSS or a system using IRS inputs), each giving a continuous indication of position relative to track.

question: In North Atlantic MNPS airspace, what must each long range navigation system provide to the crew?

options.text: A printed record of every position report made on the crossing
The fuel required to the destination
A continuous indication of position relative to track
The wind velocity at the next waypoint

explanation: Each LRNS must give the crew a continuous indication of the aircraft's position relative to track; coupling to the autopilot is highly desirable.

question: What is the Mach number technique on the North Atlantic based on?

options.text: True Mach number
The aircraft's MNE
The aircraft's MMO
Indicated Mach number

explanation: The Mach number technique used for longitudinal separation on the tracks is based on true Mach number.

question: Which letters are added after "S" in item 10 of the flight plan for an aircraft approved for both MNPS and RVSM?

options.text: W
XW
XR
X

explanation: X shows MNPS approval and W shows RVSM approval, so "XW" is inserted.

question: An aircraft in mid-ocean at 1400 local time in summer must call a station on HF. Which frequencies are most likely to work?

options.text: The higher ones, such as 13 or 17 MHz
The lower ones, such as 3 or 5 MHz, for the best range
The lowest available, below 3 MHz
Any VHF frequency above 118 MHz

explanation: By day, especially in summer, ionisation is high and the higher HF frequencies give the best long-range sky wave; lower frequencies are used at night.

question: An aircraft is cleared at Mach 0.82 and the COAT is −60°C. What is its TAS?

options.text: 466 kt
482 kt
455 kt
492 kt

explanation: Local speed of sound = 38.94 × √(273 − 60) = 568 kt. TAS = 0.82 × 568 = 466 kt.

question: Along the parallel of 57°N, about how far apart are two meridians 10° of longitude apart?

options.text: 327 NM
503 NM
285 NM
600 NM

explanation: Departure = change of longitude in minutes × cos(latitude) = 600 × cos 57° = 327 NM.

question: A twin with a one-engine-inoperative TAS of 400 kt plans an oceanic route on which no point is more than 380 NM from an adequate aerodrome. Does it need extended twin authorisation?

options.text: No, it stays within the 400 NM threshold distance
No, but only during daylight hours
Yes, because 380 NM exceeds 60 minutes at all-engines speed
Yes, all oceanic flights by twins need it

explanation: The threshold distance is 60 minutes at 400 kt = 400 NM. Staying within 380 NM of an adequate aerodrome, it does not need ETOPS authorisation.

question: At FL350 the OAT is −55°C. ATC require the aircraft to cover 520 NM in 72 minutes with a 30 kt headwind component. About what Mach number is needed?
explanation: Required GS = 520/1.2 = 433 kt, so TAS = 463 kt. Speed of sound = 38.94 × √218 = 575 kt. Mach = 463/575 = 0.81.
